l: Thespia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: Thespia is described as having temples, statues, a theatre, and a marketplace worth seeing. Its statue of Eros by Praxiteles was removed to Rome, restored to Thespia by Claudius, removed again by Nero, and eventually destroyed by fire.

l: Eros, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: Eros is especially worshipped at Thespia and by the Pariani near the Hellespont. His parentage is variously given: most people call him the son of Aphrodite, Olen calls Ilithyia his mother, and Hesiod's Theogony places him after Chaos, Earth, and Tartarus. He received statues by Lysippus, Praxiteles, and Menodorus, and was celebrated in verses by Pamphus, Orpheus, and Sappho.

l: Aphrodite, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: Praxiteles made a stone statue of Aphrodite and another of Phryne. Thespia also has a temple of Black Aphrodite.

l: Praxiteles, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: Praxiteles made a Pentelican marble statue of Eros and stone statues of Aphrodite and Phryne. The account also refers elsewhere to Phryne's ingenious trick concerning him.

l: statue of Eros by Menodorus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: The statue of Eros by Menodorus stood at Thespia in the author's day. Menodorus, an Athenian, made it as an imitation of Praxiteles's statue.

l: temple of Hercules at Thespia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: The temple has a priestess who must remain a virgin for life. One tradition connects this requirement with Hercules sparing one daughter of Thestius after sleeping with the others, but the account suggests that the temple may be too ancient for Hercules son of Amphitryon and may instead have been founded for Hercules of the Idæan Dactyli.

l: Hercules, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: One tradition says that Hercules slept with fifty daughters of Thestius in a single night, sparing one and making her the perpetual virgin priestess of his temple at Thespia. Another says that he slept with all of them and fathered sons, but the account rejects this as incredible and doubts that Hercules son of Amphitryon founded the ancient temple, suggesting instead Hercules of the Idæan Dactyli.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Helicon is described as the most fertile and tree-filled mountain in Greece, with purslane bushes that provide excellent food for goats. Its grass and roots are said not to harm humans, and its pastures make snake venom less potent. The text contrasts this with mountainous Phœnicia, where roots supposedly strengthen viper venom, and with Arabia, where vipers living near balsam trees have milder venom because they feed on the trees’ sweet-scented sap. Arabians frighten these sacred vipers away with two poles when gathering balsam sap rather than killing them.

l: Helicon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Helicon is described as the most fertile and tree-filled of the mountains of Greece. Its purslane bushes provide excellent food for goats, and its grass and roots are said not to injure humans. Its pastures make the venom of snakes less potent.

l: snakes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Snakes on Helicon are said to have less potent venom because of the mountain’s pastures. Wild snakes generally have venom that is deadly to both humans and animals.

l: venom, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: The strength of venom is said to depend greatly on the pastures where snakes live. In Helicon it is less potent, while roots in mountainous Phœnicia supposedly make viper venom more formidable; venom from vipers near balsam trees in Arabia is described as milder.

l: vipers, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Vipers in mountainous Phœnicia are said to have especially dangerous venom. In Arabia, vipers living near balsam trees are said to shelter beneath them and to have bites resembling wounds from steel, though their venom is not considered deadly because they feed on sweet-scented sap.

l: Arabia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Arabia is described as a place where vipers live near balsam trees. The vipers there feed on balsam sap, and their venom is said to have milder properties.

l: balsam trees, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Balsam trees are described as being about the size of myrtle bushes, with leaves like those of marjoram. Vipers in Arabia lodge beneath them because they enjoy their shade and feed on their sap.

l: sap of the balsam tree, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: The sap of the balsam tree is described as the food most agreeable to the vipers that live near the trees. Because the vipers feed on its sweet-scented substance, their venom is said to lose its deadly properties and become milder.

l: Arabians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Arabians gather the sap of the balsam tree when the proper season arrives. They knock two poles together to frighten away the vipers and do not kill them because they regard them as sacred.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: Ephialtes and Otus are said to have first sacrificed to the Muses on Helicon, while Ascra was built at the foot of the mountain by Œoclus and the sons of Aloeus. The sons of Aloeus believed the Muses were three, but Pierus later established nine Muses at Thespia, and other traditions describe different genealogies for them. The passage describes the fountain Aganippe, the image of Eupheme, and rites performed for Linus before sacrifices to the Muses. Linus is said to have been a renowned musician slain by Apollo, whose lament became known in Greece and Egypt, though other traditions identify different Linuses.

l: Muses, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: Ephialtes and Otus are said to have first sacrificed to the Muses on Helicon. The sons of Aloeus thought the Muses were three and called them Melete, Mneme, and Aoide, but Pierus later established nine Muses at Thespia and gave them the names they now have. Before sacrificing to the Muses, people performed annual funeral rites for Linus.

l: Helicon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: Helicon is described as a sacred mountain of the Muses, with Ascra at its foot. On the way to the grove of the Muses are the fountain Aganippe, the image of Eupheme, and a statue of Linus.

l: Ascra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: Ascra was built at the foot of Helicon by Œoclus and the sons of Aloeus, according to Hegesinous. In the author's time, only a tower remained at Ascra.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: The unit describes statues at Helicon and discusses Hesiod, Homer, Orpheus, and Dionysus. It reports several traditions about Orpheus’s powers, death, Eurydice, tomb, and remains, including accounts from Dium, the Macedonians, and Libethra. It also recounts an oracle of Dionysus predicting Libethra’s destruction after Orpheus’s remains were exposed to the Sun. The unit concludes by describing the short Orphic Hymns and their use by the Lycomidae at the Mysteries.

l: Dionysus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: Dionysus is represented at Helicon by a work of Lysippus and by an upright statue offered by Sulla and made by Myro. Dionysus in Thrace is said to have given an oracle concerning the destruction of Libethra.

l: Hesiod, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: Hesiod has a statue at Helicon showing him seated with a harp on his knees, although the text says this was not his usual appearance. His poems indicate that he sang with a laurel wand.

l: Homer, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: The text declines to decide the period of Hesiod and Homer because of the disputatiousness of those who discuss poetic subjects. The Hymns of Orpheus are said to be second only to the Hymns of Homer in composition.

l: Orpheus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: Orpheus is represented at Helicon with Telete beside him and animals listening to his singing. He is said to have excelled his predecessors in arranging poems and to have gained influence by being credited with inventing mysteries of the gods, purifications, cures, and means of turning away divine wrath. Several traditions concern his death, his connection with Eurydice, and the locations of his tomb and remains.

l: Eurydice, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: According to one account, Eurydice died before Orpheus, who went to Aornus in Thesprotia to consult an oracle of the dead about her. He thought her soul would follow him, but lost her when he turned back to look at her.

l: Thracian women, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: The Thracian women are said to have plotted against Orpheus because he persuaded their husbands to accompany him in his wanderings. After strengthening themselves with wine, they carried out the deed, and the text connects this story with the custom of men going drunk into battle.

l: Macedonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: The Macedonians who inhabit the district of Pieria say that Orpheus was slain there by women. According to an account received at Larissa, after Libethra was destroyed they removed Orpheus’s remains to Dium.

l: Dium, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: The people of Dium say that Orpheus was slain in their region and that his remains were kept there after being removed from Libethra. They also say that the river Helicon went underground so that the women who killed Orpheus could not wash away their blood-guiltiness.

l: Libethra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: Libethra was a city on Olympus where, according to an account heard at Larissa, Orpheus’s tomb was located nearby. Its people received an oracle that the city would be destroyed when the Sun saw Orpheus’s bones, and Libethra was later destroyed after his urn was broken and his remains were exposed.

l: Orpheus's tomb, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: One account places Orpheus’s tomb near Libethra, a city on Olympus. A shepherd’s singing in his sleep drew a crowd that overturned the pillar beside the tomb, exposing and breaking the urn containing Orpheus’s remains.

l: stone urn containing Orpheus's remains, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: A stone urn containing Orpheus’s remains stood on a pillar beside the road from Dium toward the mountain. The pillar was overturned by people gathering around a sleeping shepherd, the urn fell and broke, and the Sun saw the remains.

l: Orpheus's remains, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: Orpheus’s remains were said to have been kept in a stone urn near his tomb. After the urn was broken and the remains were exposed, Libethra was destroyed; the Macedonians in Dium later removed the remains to their city.

l: oracle of Dionysus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: The oracle of Dionysus in Thrace warned the people of Libethra that their city would be destroyed when the Sun saw the bones of Orpheus. They disregarded the warning because they thought a boar could not destroy the city.

l: destruction of Libethra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: The destruction of Libethra followed the exposure of Orpheus’s remains after his urn was broken. Heavy rain caused the river Sus to sweep away the city’s walls, temples, and houses and to drown its people and animals.

l: Orphic Hymns, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: The Hymns of Orpheus are described as very short and not numerous. The Lycomidae know them and chant them at the Mysteries, and they are valued for their religious spirit and considered second only to the Hymns of Homer in composition.

l: mysteries of the gods, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: Orpheus was thought to have invented the mysteries of the gods, along with purifications from unholy deeds, cures for diseases, and means of turning away the wrath of the gods.

l: Orpheus's singing, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: Orpheus’s singing is represented at Helicon by animals listening to him. A shepherd later sang some of Orpheus’s verses aloud in his sleep, drawing shepherds and husbandmen together and causing them to overturn the pillar beside Orpheus’s tomb.

l: the death of Orpheus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: Different traditions say that Orpheus was killed by Thracian women, struck by lightning from the god for revealing things in the mysteries, or that he slew himself from grief after losing Eurydice. The Macedonians of Pieria say that women killed him there.

l: Orpheus's journey to the underworld, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: The Greeks are said to believe that Orpheus went down alive to Hades to recover Eurydice from the gods of the lower world. Another account says that he went to Aornus in Thesprotia to consult an oracle of the dead about Eurydice after her death.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: At Helicon, visitors see statues, tripods, a grove dedicated to the Muses and Eros, and the spring Hippocrene. The text discusses competing traditions about Hesiod, including his works, divination, and death. It also describes the fountain of Narcissus at Donacon and competing accounts of Narcissus's love and the origin of the narcissus flower.

l: Helicon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: Mount Helicon contains the grove and festival site of the Thespians, as well as the spring Hippocrene and the small river Lamus on its summit. The surrounding traditions concern Hesiod, the Muses, Eros, and Narcissus.

l: Priapus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: Priapus has a statue at Helicon that is considered well worth seeing. He is especially honoured in places with flocks of sheep or goats or swarms of bees, and the people of Lampsacus honour him more than all the gods, saying that he is the son of Dionysus and Aphrodite.

l: Hesiod, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: Hesiod is associated with an ancient tripod said to have been awarded to him at Chalcis for a victory in song. The people around Helicon claim that he wrote only The Works and Days, while another tradition attributes several other poems to him; accounts also differ about his divination and his death.

l: Hippocrene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: Hippocrene is a spring reached after ascending twenty stades from the grove at Helicon. It is said to have been formed when the horse of Bellerophon struck the earth with its hoof, and lead bearing The Works and Days was reportedly found near it.

l: The Works and Days, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: The Works and Days is attributed by some people at Helicon as the only work written by Hesiod, with its opening address to the Muses removed so that it begins with the section about Strife. A lead copy of the poem was shown near Hippocrene, though it was almost entirely rotten with age.

l: Narcissus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: Narcissus is said to have looked into the fountain at Donacon, mistaken his reflection for another person, and died there of love. Another tradition says that he had a twin sister who resembled him, and that after her death he visited the fountain and imagined that his reflection was her image.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXII.
s: Creusis is described as a haven of the Thespians with a private statue of Dionysus, while the voyage around its coast is difficult. The coastal cities of Thisbe and Tipha are described, including their temples of Hercules and local traditions. Haliartus contains the tomb of Lysander, who died while attacking the city. Lysander is praised for his naval skill and occasional justice but condemned for executions, denying burial to captives, imposing oligarchies, and encouraging Spartan greed.

l: Creusis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXII.
s: Creusis is a haven of the Thespians with no public monuments, but a private house contains a plaster statue of Dionysus decorated with a painting. The sea voyage from the Peloponnese to Creusis is circuitous and rough because of projecting promontories and strong winds from the mountains.

l: Thisbe, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXII.
s: Thisbe is a city on the coast of Bœotia, situated beyond a coastal mountain and a plain at the foot of another mountain. It has a temple and standing stone statue of Hercules, and its inhabitants hold a festival for him; the plain nearby is kept from becoming a lake by an embankment and the diversion of water. The city is said to have taken its name from Thisbe, a local Nymph.

l: Haliartus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXII.
s: Haliartus was attacked by part of Xerxes' army during the invasion of the Medes because its people supported the Greeks. It contains the tomb of Lysander, who fell when forces from Thebes and Athens inside the city sallied out against him.

l: Lysander, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXII.
s: Lysander showed naval skill by defeating Antiochus, securing money from Cyrus, and capturing 100 Athenian ships at Ægos-potamoi while their crews were ashore. He also acted justly by condemning Eteonicus in a property dispute with Autolycus, but he was condemned for executing Philocles and 4000 Athenian captives, denying them burial, establishing Decemvirates and Harmosts, and encouraging the Lacedæmonians' desire for money. He fell while attacking Haliartus.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIII.
s: Haliartus contains Lysander’s tomb, a hero-chapel to Cecrops, the temple of the Praxidicæ, and roofless temples of uncertain dedication. Near it are Mount Tilphusium and the fountain Tilphusa, where Tiresias died after drinking while being taken to Apollo at Delphi. The river Lophis is said to have sprung from the blood of Lophis, the son of a ruler who killed him on the Pythian Priestess’s instructions. At Alalcomenae, the temple of Athene was neglected after Sulla removed its old ivory statue, and the local stream was called Triton.

l: Haliartus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIII.
s: Haliartus contains Lysander’s tomb, a hero-chapel to Cecrops, the temple of the Praxidicæ, and roofless temples whose dedications the author could not ascertain. The river Lophis flows through its district.

l: Tilphusa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIII.
s: Tilphusa is a fountain about 50 stades from Haliartus, near Mount Tilphusium. Tiresias drank from it while being taken to Apollo at Delphi and then died and was buried there.

l: Tiresias, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIII.
s: Tiresias was being taken with the spoil to Apollo at Delphi by the Argives and the sons of Polynices when he became thirsty and drank from the fountain Tilphusa. He died there and was buried on the spot.

l: Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIII.
s: Apollo was the deity to whom the Argives intended to take Tiresias and the spoil at Delphi. Manto, the daughter of Tiresias, was offered to Apollo by the Argives, and Apollo ordered her to sail to Ionia.

l: Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIII.
s: Delphi was the destination to which the Argives and the sons of Polynices were taking Tiresias and the spoil for Apollo. A ruler also went to Delphi to ask how water could be obtained in his district, and the Pythian Priestess gave him an instruction.

l: death of Tiresias, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIII.
s: Tiresias’s death occurred at the fountain Tilphusa after he drank from it while thirsty. He was buried at the fountain.

l: Lophis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIII.
s: Lophis is the river that flows through the district of Haliartus. Tradition says it was named after Lophis, whose blood caused water to gush from the ground.

l: Lophis (son of the ruler), Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIII.
s: Lophis was the son of a ruler who had gone to Delphi for instructions about obtaining water. The ruler killed him because the Pythian Priestess had ordered him to slay the first person he met on returning; Lophis, still alive, ran around, and water sprang up wherever his blood flowed.

l: Alalcomenæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIII.
s: Alalcomenae is a small village at the foot of a low mountain. It was said to have been named after Alalcomeneus, an Autochthon who reared Athene, or after Alalcomenia, one of the daughters of Ogygus.

l: Athene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIII.
s: Athene had a temple in the plain near Alalcomenae and was associated with the local river called Triton. The text says that some claimed she was brought up near the river Triton, though the author argues this should refer to the Triton in Libya rather than the local stream.

l: temple of Athene at Alalcomenae, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIII.
s: The temple of Athene near Alalcomenae contained an old ivory statue of the goddess. After Sulla removed the statue, the temple was neglected, and ivy later loosened and detached its stones.

l: old ivory statue of Athene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIII.
s: The old ivory statue of Athene stood in her temple near Alalcomenae. Sulla took it away, after which the temple was neglected.

l: Sulla, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIII.
s: Sulla removed the old ivory statue of Athene from the temple at Alalcomenae. The text criticizes his cruelty toward the Athenians, Thebans, and Orchomenians, and says that after attacking Greek cities and their gods he was afflicted with a disease that covered him with lice.

l: Triton, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIII.
s: The small torrent near Alalcomenae was called Triton because Athene was said to have been brought up near a river of that name. The author distinguishes this local stream from the Triton in Libya, which flows from Lake Tritonis into the Libyan sea.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: The text describes the temple of Itonian Athene near Coronea, where the Bœotians hold their general meeting and where Iodama was turned to stone after seeing Athene’s Gorgon-adorned tunic. It recounts features of Coronea, including altars, a temple of Hera, and nearby Mount Libethrium with statues and fountains. It also describes Mount Laphystium and the traditions of Athamas, Phrixus, Helle, and Hercules. The history of Orchomenus is traced through Andreus, Athamas, Haliartus, Coronus, Phrixus, and Eteocles.

l: Coronea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Coronea is described as having an altar of Hermes Epimelius and an altar of the Winds in its market-place. It also has a temple and ancient statue of Hera by Pythodorus the Theban, while Mount Libethrium lies about 40 stades away and Mount Laphystium about 20 stades away.

l: temple of Itonian Athene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: The temple of Itonian Athene stands between Alalcomenæ and Coronea and is the place where the Bœotians hold their general meeting. It contains brazen statues of Itonian Athene and Zeus designed by Agoracritus, as well as statues of the Graces erected during Pausanias’s time.

l: Athene Alea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Itonian Athene appeared to Iodama at night in the temple wearing a tunic bearing the head of the Gorgon Medusa. When Iodama saw it, she was turned into stone.

l: Bœotians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: The Bœotians hold their general meeting at the temple of Itonian Athene. They also say that Hercules came up from the lower world with Cerberus at Mount Laphystium.

l: Athamas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Athamas received land near Mount Laphystium, including what were later called Coronea and Haliartia, from Andreus. Believing he had no surviving male children, he adopted Haliartus and Coronus, but after Phrixus or Presbon returned, the sons of Thersander conceded Athamas’s kingdom to Phrixus and his descendants.

l: Orchomenus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Orchomenus is described as having been as famous and renowned as any Greek city. After reaching the height of prosperity, it was destined to meet an end similar to that of Mycenæ and Delos.

l: Andreus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Andreus, the son of the river Peneus, was said to have been the first to dwell at Orchomenus, whose country was then called Andreis. He married Euippe, the daughter of Leucon, at Athamas’s urging, and had a son, Eteocles.

l: Eteocles, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Eteocles became king and allowed the country to retain the name Andreis. He established the tribes Cephisias and Eteoclea, naming one after the river Cephisus and the other after himself.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: The Bœotians say that Eteocles was the first to sacrifice to the Graces and established their worship as three, although their names are not remembered. The Lacedæmonians instead say that Lacedæmon appointed two Graces, Cleta and Phaenna, while the Athenians honoured Auxo and Hegemone and later worshipped three Graces. Homer, Hesiod, and other poets give differing accounts of the Graces’ identities, names, and number. Earlier artists represented the Graces dressed, but artists in Pausanias’s time commonly represented them naked.

l: Eteocles, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: Eteocles was said by the Bœotians to have been the first to sacrifice to the Graces. He was also credited with establishing the worship of three Graces, though their names were not remembered.

l: Graces, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: The Graces were worshipped in differing numbers and under differing names: three according to Eteocles and later custom, two according to the Lacedæmonians, and with various names in Athenian and poetic traditions. Homer called one Charis and another Pasithea, while Hesiod named three as Euphrosyne, Aglaia, and Thalia.

l: Athens, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: Athens traditionally honoured the Graces Auxo and Hegemone, and also honoured the Seasons Carpo and Thallo with Pandrosus. At the entrance to the Acropolis there were three Graces, near which mysteries were celebrated, and Socrates made statues of them there for the Athenians.

l: Homer, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: Homer mentioned the Graces, calling one Charis and saying that she was the wife of Hephæstus. He also wrote that Sleep desired Pasithea, one of the younger Graces.

l: Hesiod, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: Hesiod, if he wrote the Theogony, said that the Graces were daughters of Zeus and Eurynome and named them Euphrosyne, Aglaia, and Thalia.

l: representation of the Graces, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: In more ancient times, statuaries and painters represented the Graces dressed. Examples included the golden Graces by Bupalus at Smyrna, a painted Grace by Apelles in the Odeum, Graces by Bupalus in the bed-chamber of Attalus at Pergamus, Graces by the Parian Pythagoras in the Pythium, and statues by Socrates at the entrance to the Acropolis.

l: naked representation of the Graces, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: The first person to represent the Graces naked, whether in sculpture or painting, was not known. Artists later changed the representation, and in Pausanias’s time they sculpted and painted the Graces as naked.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVI.
s: After Eteocles died without male progeny, Phlegyas succeeded to the kingdom through his mother Chryse, changed the country’s name to Phlegyantis, and established the city of Phlegyas. The people of Phlegyas separated from the other Orchomenians, attracted neighboring peoples, and were destroyed after attacking Delphi, with only a few escaping to Phocis. Chryses, son of Chrysogenia and Poseidon, succeeded the childless Phlegyas, and his son Minyas became renowned for his wealth and built a Treasury. Under Minyas’s son Orchomenus, the town and its inhabitants took the name Orchomenus and Orchomenians, while Hyettus received land there after fleeing Argos.

l: Eteocles, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVI.
s: Eteocles died without any male progeny, after which the succession passed to the posterity of Almus.

l: Almus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVI.
s: Almus had two daughters, Chrysogenia and Chryse. His descendants inherited the succession after Eteocles died.

l: Phlegyas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVI.
s: Phlegyas was the son of Chryse and Ares, and he succeeded to the kingdom after Eteocles died without male progeny. He renamed the country Phlegyantis, gave his own name to the city of Andreis, gathered the most warlike Greeks there, and died childless.

l: Orchomenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVI.
s: The Orchomenians were the broader people from whom the people of Phlegyas separated. They later continued to be distinguished from the Minyæ of Arcadia.

l: people of Phlegyas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVI.
s: The people of Phlegyas separated from the other Orchomenians, attracted neighboring peoples, and led an army against Delphi to plunder its temple. They were defeated after Philammon and some Argives came against them, and they were later overthrown by lightning, earthquakes, and an epidemic, with only a few escaping to Phocis.

l: Minyas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVI.
s: Minyas was the son of Chryses and succeeded to great wealth through his rule. His revenues surpassed those of his predecessors, and he was the first known ruler to build a Treasury for his money.

l: Minyæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVI.
s: The Minyæ took their name from Minyas. Under Orchomenus they continued to be called Minyæ in order to distinguish them from the Orchomenians in Arcadia.

l: Treasury of Minyas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVI.
s: The Treasury of Minyas was built to receive Minyas’s money. It is described as a remarkable structure that Greek historians failed to mention despite describing the Pyramids of Egypt.

l: Orchomenus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVI.
s: Orchomenus was the son of Minyas. During his reign, the town was called Orchomenus and its inhabitants were called Orchomenians; he also received Hyettus and granted him land after Hyettus fled Argos.

l: town of Orchomenus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVI.
s: During the reign of Orchomenus, the town took the name Orchomenus, and its inhabitants took the name Orchomenians. It received Hyettus as a refugee from Argos, and Orchomenus gave him the surrounding land.

l: Hyettus the Argive, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVI.
s: Hyettus fled Argos after killing Molurus, whom he had caught with his wife. Orchomenus received him and gave him the land around the village of Hyettus and the neighboring district; he is presented as the first person to take vengeance on adultery.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: Orchomenus passed to Clymenus's line after Orchomenus died without a child, but Clymenus was killed by Thebans and succeeded by Erginus. Erginus and his brothers defeated Thebes and imposed a yearly tax, which Hercules later had remitted, causing the Minyæ to suffer reverses and make peace. In old age, Erginus fathered Trophonius and Agamedes, who became renowned builders; Agamedes was killed by Trophonius during a robbery, and Trophonius was swallowed by the earth. Ascalaphus and Ialmenus later ruled the Orchomenians and led them to Troy, while Orchomenus was eventually restored after the Orchomenians were driven out by the Thebans.

l: Orchomenus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: Orchomenus had no child, so the kingdom devolved upon Clymenus, the son of Presbon. Its power was later reduced by the deity, and it was restored to the Orchomenians by Philip the son of Amyntas after they had been driven out by the Thebans.

l: Clymenus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: Clymenus was the son of Presbon and the father of Erginus, Stratius, Arrho, Pyleus, and Azeus. Some Thebans killed him at the festival of Onchestian Poseidon, after which Erginus succeeded him.

l: Erginus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: Erginus, the eldest son of Clymenus, led his brothers in war against Thebes and secured a yearly tax from the Thebans. After making peace with Hercules, he remained unmarried and childless until old age, then married a young wife according to an oracle and became the father of Trophonius and Agamedes.

l: Thebans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: The Thebans killed Clymenus over a trifling matter at the festival of Onchestian Poseidon. They were defeated by Erginus and his brothers and agreed to pay a yearly tax, which Hercules later caused to be remitted; they eventually drove the Orchomenians from their country.

l: Thebes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: Thebes was attacked by Erginus and his brothers after Clymenus was killed. Its forces were defeated, and Thebes agreed to the yearly tax for Clymenus's murder.

l: yearly tax for the murder of Clymenus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: The yearly tax was imposed on the Thebans after Erginus and his brothers defeated Thebes in retaliation for Clymenus's murder. Hercules later had the tax remitted.

l: Hercules, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: When Hercules grew up at Thebes, he had the yearly tax imposed on the Thebans remitted. The Minyæ then met with great reverses in the war, leading Erginus to make peace with him.

l: Minyæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: The Minyæ suffered great reverses in the war after Hercules had the yearly tax remitted. They were later led to Troy by Ascalaphus and Ialmenus.

l: war between the Thebans and the Minyæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: The conflict followed the imposition of the yearly tax after Clymenus's murder. The Minyæ suffered great reverses when Hercules caused the tax to be remitted, and Erginus then made peace with Hercules.

l: Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: Erginus went to Delphi to consult the oracle about obtaining offspring. The Pythian Priestess told him to put a new top on the old plough, leading him to marry a young wife.

l: Trophonius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: Trophonius was said to be the son of Apollo rather than Erginus, and the text says this is supported by consultation of the oracle of Trophonius. He became a skilled builder with Agamedes, but after cutting off Agamedes's head, he was swallowed by the earth in the grove of Lebadea.

l: Agamedes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: Agamedes was the son of Erginus and brother of Trophonius. He became a skilled builder, helped construct temples and palaces, and was trapped while robbing Hyrieus's treasury; Trophonius cut off his head.

l: Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: Apollo was said to be the father of Trophonius, contrary to the account that named Erginus as Trophonius's father. Trophonius and Agamedes were credited with building Apollo's temple at Delphi.

l: Ascalaphus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: Ascalaphus was reputed to be a son of Ares by Astyoche, the daughter of Azeus. He ruled over the Orchomenians with Ialmenus and led the Minyæ to Troy.

l: Ialmenus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: Ialmenus was reputed to be a son of Ares by Astyoche, the daughter of Azeus. He ruled over the Orchomenians with Ascalaphus and led the Minyæ to Troy.

l: Orchomenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: The Orchomenians were ruled by Ascalaphus and Ialmenus, who led them to Troy. They later joined the expedition to Ionia with the sons of Codrus, were driven from their country by the Thebans, and were restored to Orchomenus by Philip the son of Amyntas.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: Orchomenus contains temples, sacred stones, the treasury and tomb of Minyas, the tomb of Hesiod, and monuments associated with Actaeon and Hercules. The Pythian Priestess instructed the Orchomenians to recover Hesiod’s bones from Naupactus and later to bury Actaeon’s remains and fasten a brazen image of his spectre to a stone. Hercules was credited by the Thebans with diverting the Cephisus into the Orchomenian plain and blocking its former outlet, though the text questions whether the Orchomenians could not have reversed this work. Chersias described the ancestry of Aspledon and was said to have composed Hesiod’s epitaph.

l: Orchomenus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: Orchomenus has a temple of Dionysus, an ancient temple of the Graces, sacred meteoric stones, a well, the treasury of Minyas, and the tombs of Minyas and Hesiod. Its people recovered Hesiod’s bones from Naupactus after consulting Delphi, annually offer funeral rites to Actaeon, and say that Aspledon lost its inhabitants through lack of water.

l: Treasury of Minyas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: The treasury of Minyas at Orchomenus is described as a circular stone building with a not very pointed top. Its highest stone is said to hold the whole structure together, and it is called a marvel inferior to nothing in Greece or elsewhere.

l: Minyas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: Minyas has a tomb at Orchomenus. The Orchomenians are called Minyae in the inscription concerning Hesiod’s remains.

l: Hesiod, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: Hesiod has a tomb at Orchomenus, where his bones were brought from Naupactus after a pestilence. The bones were found in a hollow stone identified by a crow, and an elegiac inscription says that Ascra was his fatherland and that the Minyae received his remains.

l: Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: The Orchomenians consulted Delphi during a pestilence that destroyed people and cattle and again about where Hesiod’s bones could be found. They also consulted Delphi when a spectre injured their land.

l: Pythian Priestess, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: The Pythian Priestess instructed the Orchomenians to bring Hesiod’s bones from Naupactus to Orchomenus as a remedy for pestilence. When asked where the bones were, she said that a crow would show them; concerning Actaeon, she ordered them to bury his remains and fasten a brazen copy of the spectre to a stone.

l: Actæon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: Actaeon is associated at Orchomenus with a spectre that injured the land. The Orchomenians buried whatever remains of him they could find and annually offer him funeral rites.

l: spectre of Actaeon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: A spectre associated with Actaeon sat on a stone and injured the land of Orchomenus. The Orchomenians made a brazen copy of it and fastened the copy with iron to the stone.

l: Hercules, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: Hercules has a temple and small statue about seven stades from Orchomenus. The Thebans say that he diverted the river Cephisus into the Orchomenian plain and dammed its passage to the sea under the mountain.

l: lake Cephisis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: The lake Cephisis receives the river Melas and covers a large part of the Orchomenian district. In winter, when the South Wind generally prevails, its water spreads over most of the country; Homer knows of the lake but not as a creation of Hercules.

l: Cephisus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: The river Cephisus was said by the Thebans to have been diverted by Hercules into the Orchomenian plain. Its former outlet to the sea under the mountain was allegedly blocked by Hercules.

l: Homer, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: Homer mentions the lake Cephisis as an existing feature but does not say that Hercules made it. He also indicates that much wealth came to Orchomenus in the period of the Trojan War.

l: Chersias, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: Chersias, an Orchomenian, wrote verses stating that Aspledon was the son of Poseidon and the Nymph Midea and was born in the large city. Callippus cited these verses, and the Orchomenians say that Chersias composed the epitaph on Hesiod.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIX.
s: Lebadea is described as a prosperous town whose grove of Trophonius contains temples, statues, caves, and the sources of the River Hercyna. The account explains the origins of Hercyna and describes Trophonius’s oracle, including the sacrifices, purification, descent into the artificial underground chamber, and methods of receiving answers. Consultors drink from the waters of Lethe and Memory, descend with honey cakes, and are questioned after returning. The narrative also records that the author personally witnessed people consult the oracle and had consulted it himself.

l: Lebadea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIX.
s: Lebadea was originally built on high ground and called Midea, but its inhabitants later descended to the plain after Lebadus came from Athens and settled there. The town was named Lebadea after him and is said to be adorned like the most famous Greek towns.

l: Grove of Trophonius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIX.
s: The grove of Trophonius lies some distance from Lebadea and contains the temple of Trophonius, a temple of Demeter called Europa, a statue of Zeus Hyetius, Proserpine’s Chase, a temple of Zeus the King, temples of Cronos, Hera, Zeus, and Apollo, and the tomb of Arcesilaus.

l: Trophonius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIX.
s: Trophonius is associated with an oracle at Lebadea, where visitors sacrifice to him and descend into an underground sanctuary to learn the future. Dragons are said to be especially sacred to him, and Demeter called Europa is said to have been his nurse.

l: Proserpine, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIX.
s: Proserpine, the daughter of Demeter, was playing with Hercyna when a goose hid under a stone in a cave. Proserpine entered the cave, took up the stone, and caused water to burst forth, after which the river was called Hercyna.

l: Demeter, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIX.
s: Demeter has a temple in the grove called Europa, and she is said to have been the nurse of Trophonius. Those preparing to descend to Trophonius sacrifice to Demeter under this name.

l: River Hercyna, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIX.
s: The River Hercyna is said to have sprung up when Proserpine took a stone from a cave while retrieving a goose. Its sources are in the cave, and a temple of Hercyna with the effigy of a maiden holding a goose stands on its banks; those preparing for the oracle bathe in the river.

l: Temple of Trophonius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIX.
s: The temple of Trophonius is among the principal features of the grove. It contains a statue like Æsculapius, made by Praxiteles.

l: oracle of Trophonius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIX.
s: The oracle of Trophonius is situated above the grove on the mountain inside a small circular stone wall with brazen pillars, girders, and doors. Its artificial chamber is shaped like an oven, is about four cubits wide and eight cubits deep, and has a narrow opening through which the consulter is drawn after lying flat and presenting his feet, knees, body, and honey cakes.

l: Temple of the Good Deity and Good Fortune, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIX.
s: A person seeking the oracle must first stay for several days in the temple of the Good Deity and Good Fortune. After returning from the sanctuary, the person is brought back there while still terrified and confused, and later is said to recover and laugh about the experience.

l: sacrificial ritual for Trophonius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIX.
s: Before descending, the consulter purifies himself, avoids warm baths, bathes in the River Hercyna, and receives animal food from various victims. Sacrifices are made to Trophonius and his sons, Apollo, Cronos, Zeus the King, Hera the Chariot-driver, and Demeter called Europa, with a seer inspecting the entrails; on the night of descent, a ram is sacrificed in a ditch while Agamedes is invoked, and its entrails must be favorable.

l: oracle consultation and descent, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIX.
s: Two thirteen-year-old citizen lads called Hermæ wash and otherwise attend the consulter, who then drinks from the waters of Lethe and Memory, worships a statue said to have been made by Dædalus, and approaches the oracle at night in a linen tunic, fillets, and local shoes. Inside, the future is communicated to some through their eyes and to others through their ears; after returning, the priests seat the consulter on the Seat of Memory, ask what was seen or heard, and have the account written on a tablet.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: The Bœotians, suffering a two-year drought, were directed by the oracle at Delphi to seek Trophonius at Lebadea, where Saon from Acræphnium discovered the oracle and learned its ritual. The text lists works attributed to Dædalus in Bœotia, Crete, Delos, Argos, and Sicily, and describes the origins and history of Chæronea. Sulla and the Romans erected trophies at Chæronea for victories over Taxilus and the army of Mithridates, while Philip son of Amyntas erected no trophies. Near Chæronea stands the common sepulchre of the Thebans who fell in the battle against Philip, and the people of Chæronea chiefly venerate the sceptre of Zeus, which they call the spear.

l: Bœotians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: After two years without rain, the Bœotians sent messengers from every city to consult the oracle at Delphi. They were directed to go to Trophonius at Lebadea to obtain a cure for the drought.

l: Bœotia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: Bœotia contains two works attributed to Dædalus: the Hercules at Thebes and the Trophonius at Lebadea.

l: the drought, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: The drought lasted for two years without rain, leading the Bœotians to consult Delphi and seek a cure from Trophonius.

l: Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: The Bœotians sent messengers to Delphi, whose Pythian Priestess directed them to Trophonius at Lebadea.

l: Trophonius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: Trophonius was sought at Lebadea as the source of a cure for the Bœotian drought. He instructed Saon from Acræphnium in all the ritual and routine of his oracle.

l: Lebadea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: At Lebadea, the Bœotian messengers initially could not find the oracle of Trophonius. The place is also associated with a work of Dædalus representing Trophonius.

l: the oracle of Trophonius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: The oracle was discovered when Saon from Acræphnium followed a swarm of bees into the ground. Saon was then instructed in its ritual and routine by Trophonius.

l: Saon from Acræphnium, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: Saon, the oldest of the Bœotian messengers, followed a swarm of bees and thereby discovered the oracle of Trophonius at Lebadea. Trophonius instructed him in the oracle’s ritual and routine.

l: Dædalus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: Dædalus was credited with works including the Hercules at Thebes, the Trophonius at Lebadea, the Britomartis at Olus, the Athene at Gnossus, and a dancing-ground of Ariadne in Crete. A wooden statue of Aphrodite at Delos was also attributed to him, while his works dedicated by the Argives in the temple of Hera and those brought to Gela from Omphace had been effaced by time.

l: Chæronea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: Chæronea was said in ancient times to have been called Arne and to have received its later name from Chæron, son of Apollo and Thero. It had two trophies erected by Sulla and the Romans, and near it stood the common sepulchre of the Thebans who fell against Philip.

l: Sulla, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: Sulla erected a trophy at Chæronea for victory over Taxilus and the army of Mithridates.

l: Romans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: The Romans erected a trophy at Chæronea for victory over Taxilus and the army of Mithridates.

l: Philip the son of Amyntas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: Philip son of Amyntas erected no trophy at Chæronea or elsewhere for victories over Greeks or barbarians. The text contrasts this with the trophies of Sulla and the Romans.

l: the battle against Philip, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: The battle against Philip resulted in the deaths of Thebans whose remains were placed in a common sepulchre near Chæronea.

l: the common sepulchre of the Thebans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: The common sepulchre of the Thebans who fell in the battle against Philip stood as Chæronea was approached. It had no inscription but displayed a lion, which may have indicated their bravery.

l: Thebans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: The Thebans who fell in the battle against Philip were buried in a common sepulchre near Chæronea. Their sepulchre bore a lion but no inscription.

l: sceptre of Agamemnon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: The people of Chæronea venerated most the sceptre that Hephæstus made for Zeus and that passed through Hermes, Pelops, Atreus, and Thyestes to Agamemnon. They called it the spear, kept it in a certain building, sacrificed to it daily, and spread a table of meats and pastry for it each year through its priest.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLI.
s: The text discusses works attributed to Hephæstus, especially the sceptre of Agamemnon, which is considered probably the only one of his works still extant. It compares several other objects claimed to be made by Hephæstus, including a brazen bowl at Patara and a chest at Patræ, while questioning the identity of the necklace displayed at Amathus. It relates the necklace’s association with Harmonia and Eriphyle, its dedication at Delphi, and its later seizure by Phocian tyrants. The text also describes Petrachos above Chæronea and the healing unguents made at Chæronea from flowers.

l: Hephæstus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLI.
s: Hephæstus is credited with making the sceptre of Agamemnon, a brazen bowl shown at Patara, and a chest brought from Troy by Eurypylus. The text concludes that the sceptre is probably the only work of Hephæstus still extant.

l: sceptre of Agamemnon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLI.
s: The sceptre of Agamemnon is described as certainly being the work of Hephæstus. It is regarded as probably the only work of Hephæstus still extant.

l: Amathus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLI.
s: Amathus is a city in Cyprus with an ancient temple of Adonis and Aphrodite. The temple contains a necklace said to have originally been given to Harmonia and called the necklace of Eriphyle.

l: necklace of Eriphyle, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLI.
s: The necklace given to Harmonia was later called the necklace of Eriphyle because Eriphyle received it as a gift from her husband. The sons of Phegeus dedicated it at Delphi, and it was later carried off by the Phocian tyrants.

l: Eriphyle, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLI.
s: Eriphyle received the necklace associated with Harmonia as a gift from her husband. The text cites Homer as saying that she sold her husband for gold and says that her necklace was entirely gold.

l: necklace at Amathus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLI.
s: The necklace at Amathus is said to be the necklace originally given to Harmonia and later called Eriphyle’s necklace. The text doubts that it is the same necklace, because the one at Amathus consists of emeralds set in gold, whereas Eriphyle’s is said by Homer to have been entirely gold.

l: Petrachos, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLI.
s: Petrachos is a crag above Chæronea. It is said to be the place where Cronos was deceived by Rhea with a stone instead of Zeus, and a small statue of Zeus stands on its summit.

l: Chæronea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLI.
s: At Chæronea, unguents are made by boiling together lilies, roses, narcissuses, and irises. The town is also associated with Petrachos, the crag above it.

l: unguents made at Chæronea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLI.
s: The unguents made at Chæronea are said to relieve pain. When an unguent made from roses is applied to wooden statues, it preserves them from rotting.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK X.--PHOCIS. / CHAPTER I.
s: Phocis is described as a region near Bœotia, the Peloponnese, and the sea, whose inhabitants fought several wars against the Thessalians. The Phocians first defeated Thessalian cavalry at Hyampolis by burying earthenware pots in the ground, and later won a major battle after receiving an oracle from Delphi and preparing to sacrifice their women, children, and possessions if defeated. Tellias of Elis commanded the Phocians and later devised a successful night attack in which 500 Phocians covered themselves and their armour with plaster to resemble a divine apparition. The Phocians commemorated their victory by sending statues of Tellias, other commanders, and local heroes to Apollo at Delphi.

l: Phocis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK X.--PHOCIS. / CHAPTER I.
s: Phocis is described as lying opposite the Peloponnese, near Bœotia, and on the sea, with ports at Cirrha and Anticyra. Its inhabitants fought the Thessalians and achieved notable victories through stratagems and determined resistance.

l: Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK X.--PHOCIS. / CHAPTER I.
s: Delphi was the place to which the Phocians sent to learn how they could escape the danger posed by the Thessalians. The Phocians later sent statues of their commanders and local heroes to Apollo at Delphi.

l: Hyampolis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK X.--PHOCIS. / CHAPTER I.
s: Hyampolis was the place where the Phocians buried earthenware pots to obstruct the attacking Thessalian cavalry. The Phocians also associated Hyampolis with Daiphantes, who commanded their cavalry in the later battle.

l: Phocians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK X.--PHOCIS. / CHAPTER I.
s: The Phocians fought the Thessalians with stratagems, including buried pots and a night attack by men covered in plaster. After suffering the loss of Gelon and 300 picked men, they prepared to sacrifice their women, children, and possessions if defeated, but they won a famous victory under their commanders and Tellias of Elis.

l: Thessalians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK X.--PHOCIS. / CHAPTER I.
s: The Thessalians attacked the Phocians at Hyampolis and suffered losses when their horses encountered buried earthenware pots. They later invaded Phocis with forces from all their cities, killed Gelon and 300 Phocian men, and were subsequently defeated in battle and in a later night attack.

l: earthenware pots, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK X.--PHOCIS. / CHAPTER I.
s: The Phocians buried earthenware pots in the ground at the place where they expected the Thessalian cavalry to attack. The pots lamed some horses and caused some Thessalian riders to be killed or thrown from their horses.

l: Thessalian cavalry, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK X.--PHOCIS. / CHAPTER I.
s: The Thessalian cavalry charged over the concealed earthenware pots at Hyampolis, suffering lamed horses, killed riders, and men who were unhorsed. It later helped kill Gelon and the 300 picked Phocians.

l: Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK X.--PHOCIS. / CHAPTER I.
s: Apollo gave the Phocians an oracle concerning their danger through Delphi. After their victory, the Phocians sent him statues of Tellias, the other commanders, and local heroes.

l: oracle concerning the Phocians' danger, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK X.--PHOCIS. / CHAPTER I.
s: The oracle said that a mortal and an immortal would be put together in combat, with victory given to both but the greater victory to the mortal. It became clear to the Greeks after the Phocians won, because the Thessalian word was Itonian Athene and the Phocian word was Phocus.

l: Gelon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK X.--PHOCIS. / CHAPTER I.
s: Gelon led 300 picked Phocians against the Thessalians at night, with orders to observe stealthily and avoid fighting if possible. The Thessalians killed Gelon and all the men with him, riding them down and butchering them.

l: Phocian women and children, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK X.--PHOCIS. / CHAPTER I.
s: The Phocians gathered their women and children before the decisive battle. They ordered that, if the Phocians were defeated, the women and children should be killed and offered as victims.

l: funeral pile, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK X.--PHOCIS. / CHAPTER I.
s: The Phocians built a large funeral pile containing their gathered possessions, including apparel, gold, silver, and statues of the gods. Thirty men were ordered to kill the women and children, burn the pile, and either kill one another or attack the Thessalian cavalry if the Phocians lost.

l: Tellias of Elis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK X.--PHOCIS. / CHAPTER I.
s: Tellias of Elis was the Phocians' seer and commander in chief, and their hopes for safety rested on him. He helped secure the Phocian victory and later devised the night attack in which the Phocians smeared themselves and their armour with plaster.

l: battle between the Phocians and Thessalians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK X.--PHOCIS. / CHAPTER I.
s: The battle was commanded for the Phocians by Rhœus of Ambrosus and Daiphantes of Hyampolis, with Tellias of Elis as commander in chief. The Phocians fought in desperation after preparing for the possible destruction of their women, children, and possessions, and they won a famous victory.

l: Phocian victory over the Thessalians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK X.--PHOCIS. / CHAPTER I.
s: The Phocians' victory was aided by their desperation and by auspicious omens from the god. They commemorated it by sending statues of Tellias, the other commanders, and local heroes to Apollo at Delphi.

l: night attack on the Thessalians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK X.--PHOCIS. / CHAPTER I.
s: Five hundred picked Phocians launched the night attack when the moon was full after the Thessalian camp had been pitched at the entrance to Phocis. They covered themselves and their armour with plaster so that they looked white, causing a tremendous slaughter because the Thessalians mistook them for a divine appearance.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: The Phocians, led first by Philomelus, seized the temple at Delphi after being fined by the Amphictyonic Council and recruited a strong mercenary army. The Thebans declared war on them, and the conflict lasted ten years with victories on both sides until the Phocians were defeated near Neon and Philomelus died. Onomarchus then commanded the Phocians, but after Philip the son of Amyntas joined the Thebans and defeated them, Onomarchus was killed by his own soldiers. Phayllus and then Phalæcus succeeded him, but both later died or lost power amid divine retribution and the misuse of sacred money.

l: Phocians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: The Phocians were reportedly compelled to join Xerxes when the Persians entered Europe, but they deserted the Medes and fought for the Greeks at Platæa. Later, after a fine was imposed on them by the Amphictyonic Council, they seized the temple at Delphi, raised a large mercenary army, and fought the Thebans for ten years. They were eventually defeated near Neon, and their later commanders suffered death or deposition.

l: Amphictyonic Council, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: The Amphictyonic Council imposed a fine on the Phocians for reasons the author could not ascertain. After the seizure of the temple at Delphi, it was said to have imposed the same death suffered by Philomelus on all who had plundered the temple.

l: Philomelus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: Philomelus, son of Philotimus and a native of Ledon, persuaded the Phocians that they could not pay their fine and urged them to seize the temple at Delphi. He led the Phocians at the beginning of their war with the Thebans, but after their defeat near Neon he threw himself from a steep crag and died.

l: Thebans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: The Thebans had previously been at variance with the Phocians and openly declared war on them after the temple at Delphi was seized. They fought the Phocians for ten years, sometimes prevailing and sometimes being defeated, and later received the support of Philip the son of Amyntas.

l: Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: At Delphi, Heraclides was President when the Phocians seized the temple. The site contained, among Apollo's votive offerings, a brass imitation of an emaciated old man that was said to have been given by Hippocrates the doctor.

l: temple at Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: The Phocians seized the temple at Delphi after Philomelus persuaded them that they could not pay their fine. The seizure led to war with the Thebans, and the Amphictyonic Council condemned those who plundered the temple to the same end as Philomelus.

l: war between the Phocians and the Thebans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: The war lasted ten continuous years, during which the Phocians and their mercenaries and the Thebans repeatedly prevailed over one another. The conflict turned against the Phocians in an engagement near Neon, where they were routed.

l: Onomarchus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: After Philomelus's death, the Phocians appointed Onomarchus to command them. After Philip the son of Amyntas joined the Thebans and defeated him, Onomarchus fled toward the sea and was shot by his own soldiers, who blamed the defeat on his cowardice and inexperience.

l: Philip the son of Amyntas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: Philip the son of Amyntas joined the Thebans and defeated the Phocians in battle. His victory led to Onomarchus's flight and death.

l: Phayllus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: After Onomarchus died, the Phocians chose his brother Phayllus as commander in chief with unlimited power. Phayllus dreamed that he had become like a wasting brass image of an old man among Apollo's offerings, and a wasting disease soon afflicted him and fulfilled the dream.

l: Phalæcus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: After Phayllus died, power in Phocis passed to his son Phalæcus. Phalæcus was deposed for privately taking sacred money, then went to Crete with his supporters and some mercenaries; while besieging Cydonia, he lost most of his army and his own life.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Philip ended the Phocian or Sacred War in the tenth year after the temple was plundered, during the archonship of Theophilus at Athens and the first year of the 108th Olympiad. Many Phocian towns were destroyed, and the Phocians were deprived of participation in the temple at Delphi and in the general Greek Council, while their votes in the Amphictyonic Council were given to the Macedonians. The Athenians and Thebans later helped rebuild the Phocian towns before the fatal Greek defeat at the Battle of Chæronea. The Phocians subsequently fought against Antipater and the Macedonians at Lamia and Crannon and against the Galati and the Celtic army at Delphi.

l: Philip, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Philip put an end to the Phocian or Sacred War in its tenth year after the plunder of the temple.

l: Sacred War, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: The Phocian or Sacred War ended when Philip brought it to a close. It had followed the plunder of the temple and resulted in the destruction of many Phocian towns and the political punishment of the Phocians.

l: Phocians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: The Phocians were deprived of participation in the temple at Delphi and in the general Greek Council, and their votes in the Amphictyonic Council were given to the Macedonians. Their towns were later rebuilt with help from the Athenians and Thebans, and the Phocians fought at Chæronea, against Antipater and the Macedonians at Lamia and Crannon, and against the Galati and the Celtic army at Delphi.

l: Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Delphi was the site of the temple connected with the Phocians' punishment and later the place where they fought the Galati and the Celtic army.

l: temple of Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: The temple at Delphi had been plundered before Philip ended the war. The Phocians were thereafter deprived of participation in it, and their seizure of the temple was cited as part of their guilt.

l: Macedonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: The Macedonians received the Phocians' votes in the Amphictyonic Council. The Phocians later fought against the Macedonians at Lamia and Crannon.

l: Phocian towns, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Many Phocian towns were taken and razed to the ground, including Lilæa, Hyampolis, Anticyra, Parapotamii, Panopeus, and Daulis. The towns were later rebuilt and repopulated from the villages, except for places that remained weak because of a lack of money.

l: Athenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: The Athenians helped restore the Phocian towns before the fatal defeat of the Greeks at Chæronea.

l: Thebans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: The Thebans helped restore the Phocian towns before the fatal defeat of the Greeks at Chæronea.

l: Greeks, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: The Greeks suffered a fatal defeat at Chæronea, in which the Phocians took part.

l: battle of Chæronea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: The Battle of Chæronea is described as the fatal defeat of the Greeks. The Phocians participated in it, after the Athenians and Thebans had helped restore the Phocian towns.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IV.
s: Panopeus is a small settlement in Phocis, about 20 stades from Chæronea, whose inhabitants live in narrow dwellings but participate in the Phocian Council. Its traditions connect it with Phlegyans, Prometheus, Tityus, and the dances of the Thyiades. Nearby Daulis is a small but physically strong Phocian town associated with the myths of Tereus, Procne, and Philomela, and with a hero-chapel at Tronis.

l: Panopeus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IV.
s: Panopeus is a town in Phocis with no town-hall, gymnasium, theatre, market-place, or public fountain; its inhabitants live in narrow dwellings near a ravine, but it has boundaries and sends members to the Phocian Council. It is said to have been named after the father of Epeus, while another tradition says its inhabitants were Phlegyans who fled from Orchomenia. Its ancient enclosure is estimated at about seven stades, and the Thyiades hold dances there.

l: Phocis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IV.
s: Phocis contains Panopeus and Daulis, and Panopeus sends members to the Phocian Council. The Bœotians have their easiest approach to Phocis through the point near Panopeus.

l: Tityus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IV.
s: Tityus is associated with a sepulchre near the ravine at Panopeus, whose mound has a circumference of about a third of a stade. Homer describes him as lying across nine roods, though some interpret the passage as naming the place where he lay; Cleon claimed that Tityus and others may have been as large as tradition represented.

l: Thyiades, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IV.
s: The Thyiades are Athenian women who annually go to Parnassus with the Delphian women to celebrate the orgies of Dionysus. They hold dances on the road from Athens and elsewhere, including Panopeus, which explains Homer’s description of Panopeus as delighting in the dance.

l: Prometheus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IV.
s: Prometheus is identified by some as the figure represented by a Pentelican marble statue in a building at Panopeus. Stones near the ravine, resembling clay and smelling like the human body, are said to be remains of the clay from which Prometheus fashioned the human race.

l: Daulis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IV.
s: Daulis is about seven stades from Panopeus, though the distance may be corrupt, and its inhabitants are few but renowned among the Phocians for their size and strength. The town is said to have been named after the nymph Daulis, daughter of Cephisus, or after the dense trees once found there. It contains a temple and ancient statue of Athene, an older wooden statue said to have been brought by Procne, and the nearby place called Tronis, where a hero-chapel was built.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: The unit describes the road from Daulis to Delphi, including the Phocian assembly building and the Cross-roads where Oedipus is said to have killed his father. It recounts traditions about the origins and succession of the oracle of Apollo, involving Earth, Poseidon, Themis, Apollo, Daphnis, Phemonoe, Olen, and others. It also gives several traditions about Delphi’s successive temples, ending with the stone temple built by the Amphictyones after the fourth temple burned down.

l: Daulis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Daulis is the starting point for an ascent to the heights of Parnassus and lies on the high road to Delphi. After leaving Daulis, travelers reach the Phocicum on the left side of the road.

l: Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: The high road from the Cross-roads to Delphi is very steep and difficult even for a well-equipped traveler. Delphi is associated with many traditions about the oracle of Apollo and the successive temples built there.

l: Cross-roads, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: The Cross-roads are said to be the place where Oedipus murdered his father. The tombs of Laius and his attendant stand in the middle of the place where the three roads meet.

l: Œdipus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Oedipus is said to have murdered his father at the Cross-roads in Phocis. His later woes are attributed to this deed and to the Cross-roads, while he was also exposed on Mount Cithaeron after his ankles were pierced and was brought up at Corinth.

l: oracle of Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: The oracle of Apollo at Delphi has several reported origins and successions. Phemonoe is regarded as its first priestess and the first to recite its oracles in hexameters, while other traditions associate its earliest prophetic figures with Daphnis, Olen, shepherds, and others.

l: Earth, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Earth is said to have possessed the earliest oracle at Delphi and to have appointed Daphnis, one of the Mountain Nymphs, as its priestess. In the Eumolpia, Earth shares the oracle with Poseidon, later gives her share to Themis, and ultimately Apollo receives it from Themis.

l: Poseidon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Poseidon is represented in the Eumolpia as sharing the oracle at Delphi with Earth and employing Pyrcon as his interpreter. He later receives Calauria near Troezen as his share in exchange for the oracle.

l: Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Apollo receives Earth’s share of the oracle from Themis and becomes the god associated with the Delphic oracle. He is also said to have sent the second temple, made of wax and bees’ wings, to the Hyperboreans.

l: first temple of Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: The first temple of Apollo is said to have been built from laurel branches brought from a tree at Tempe, making it resemble a hut.

l: fourth temple of Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: The fourth temple of Apollo was built of stone by Trophonius and Agamedes. It burned down when Erxiclides was Archon at Athens, in the first year of the 58th Olympiad.

l: Amphictyones, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: The Amphictyones built the temple that still exists at Delphi using sacred money. Its architect was the Corinthian Spintharus.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: The unit recounts several traditions about the origins and names of Parnassus, Lycorea, Delphi, and Pytho. Parnassus is said to have founded the earliest town there, which was destroyed in Deucalion’s flood, after which survivors founded Lycorea. Other traditions connect Lycorea, the Corycian cavern, and Delphi with Apollo and various divine or heroic figures. Pytho was traditionally named for the dragon slain by Apollo, who was said to guard Earth’s oracle, and Phemonoe later delivered an oracle promising Apollo’s protection of the Delphians.

l: Parnassus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: Parnassus is said to have been the son of the Nymph Cleodora and to have had Poseidon as his divine father and Cleopompus as his human father. He supposedly built the most ancient town there, discovered omens from the flight of birds, and gave his name to Mount Parnassus and the dell Parnassus.

l: Parnassus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: Mount Parnassus is said to have been named after Parnassus. After Deucalion’s flood, the human beings who escaped it followed wolves and other wild beasts to the top of Mount Parnassus.

l: Deucalion’s flood, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: Deucalion’s flood is said to have destroyed the town built by Parnassus. The human beings who escaped the flood followed wolves and other wild beasts to Mount Parnassus and founded Lycorea.

l: Lycorea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: Lycorea was supposedly founded by the survivors of Deucalion’s flood after they followed wolves to Mount Parnassus, and its name was associated with this circumstance as Wolf-town. Another tradition says that Lycorea was named after Lycorus, who was the son of Apollo and the Nymph Corycia.

l: Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: Apollo is named in several traditions about the origins of the region and its names. He was said to be the father of Lycorus, Delphus, and possibly Delphus by Thyia, and he slew the dragon with his arrows; Phemonoe’s oracle also promised that Apollo would protect the Delphians from a plunderer.

l: Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: Delphi was said to have received its name from Delphus, whose parentage is given differently in several traditions. Its inhabitants later called the town both Pytho and Delphi, and its priestess Phemonoe delivered an oracle concerning Apollo’s defense of the Delphians.

l: Pytho, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
