s: Pytho was another name used by the inhabitants for Delphi. Some genealogists attributed the name to Pythes, the son of Delphus, but the prevalent tradition connected it with the dragon that Apollo slew, because the dragon rotted there.

l: dragon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: The dragon was said by the poets to have been placed there by Earth to guard her oracle. Apollo slew it with his arrows, and its rotting was traditionally given as the reason the town was called Pytho.

l: oracle, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: The dragon was said to guard Earth’s oracle before Apollo slew it. When the Delphians sought Apollo’s protection from a plundering son of Crius, Phemonoe, who was then priestess, delivered an oracle in hexameters promising that Apollo would send his heavy arrow against the man.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: The temple at Delphi was repeatedly plundered, most extensively by the Phocian authorities and the army of the Galati, and finally by Nero, who removed 500 bronze statues dedicated to Apollo. The earliest contest at Delphi was singing a hymn in honour of Apollo, and later the Amphictyones added musical, athletic, and equestrian events. The Pythian games gradually introduced new contests, while singing to the pipes was discontinued because its music was considered gloomy. Victors in the Pythian games received a laurel crown, associated with Apollo's reported love for Daphne, daughter of Ladon.

l: temple at Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: The temple at Delphi was plundered from the beginning by an Euboean robber, the people of Phlegyas, Pyrrhus son of Achilles, part of Xerxes' army, the Phocian authorities, the Galati, and finally Nero. Nero carried off 500 bronze statues from Apollo, depicting both gods and men.

l: Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: Delphi was the site of the musical and athletic contests later known as the Pythian games. Homer went there to ask what was necessary for him, and the temple there was repeatedly plundered.

l: Phocian General Council, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Phocian authorities were among those who enriched themselves most and longest from the treasures of the god at Delphi.

l: Galati, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: The army of the Galati was among those who enriched themselves most and longest by plundering the treasures of the god at Delphi.

l: Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: Apollo's temple at Delphi was plundered repeatedly, and Nero removed 500 bronze statues from it. The earliest contest at Delphi honored Apollo through the singing of a hymn, and the laurel crown was associated with his reported love for Daphne.

l: musical contest at Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: The earliest contest at Delphi was a musical contest for singing a hymn in honour of Apollo. Later, contests were established for harping, pipes, singing to the pipes, and harping without vocal accompaniment.

l: singing a Hymn in honour of Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: Singing a Hymn in honour of Apollo was said to be the most ancient contest at Delphi and the first contest for which a prize was given. Chrysothemis the Cretan was its first reported victor, followed by Philammon and then his son Thamyris.

l: Amphictyones, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: In the third year of the 48th Olympiad, the Amphictyones established prizes for harping and added contests for pipes and singing to the pipes. They later introduced athletic contests, a chariot race, harping without vocal accompaniment, and additional racing events, while changing the Pythian contest from prize competitions to contests for a crown in the second Pythiad.

l: Pythian games, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Pythian games began with singing a hymn in honour of Apollo and later included musical, athletic, chariot, and horse-racing contests. Over time, the games discontinued singing to the pipes, introduced contests such as the race in armour and the pancratium for boys, and awarded victors a laurel crown.

l: singing to the pipes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: Singing to the pipes was added as a Pythian contest in the third year of the 48th Olympiad, with Echembrotus of Arcadia named as victor. It was discontinued in the second Pythiad because the music was considered the most gloomy kind, and because elegies and dirges were sung in that manner.

l: chariot race, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: A chariot race was later added to the Pythian contests, and Clisthenes the tyrant of Sicyon was proclaimed its victor. The games subsequently included races for a pair-horse chariot, a chariot with colts, a pair of colts, and a racing colt.

l: crown of laurel, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: Victors in the Pythian games received a crown of laurel. The text says this was probably because Apollo was reportedly enamoured of Daphne, daughter of Ladon.

l: Daphne, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: Daphne, the daughter of Ladon, was associated with the laurel because Apollo was reportedly enamoured of her. The text also notes that the name Daphne means laurel.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The unit describes the origins and changing membership of the general Council of the Greeks, later called the Amphictyonic Council, including the roles of the Phocians, Macedonians, Lacedæmonians, and Nicopolis. It recounts how Augustus altered the distribution of votes and states that the Amphictyones numbered thirty in the narrator’s time. It then describes four temples at Delphi, including the temple of Athene Pronoia, the Massaliotes’ votive offering, and the former golden shield of Crœsus. The unit also discusses the hero Phylacus, the river Plistus, and the origins and properties of the Castalia spring.

l: general Council of the Greeks, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Some people say that Amphictyon, the son of Deucalion, appointed the general Council of the Greeks. Androtion instead says that delegates originally came to Delphi from neighboring people called Amphictiones.

l: Amphictyones, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The Amphictyones were originally delegates from neighboring peoples who assembled at Delphi, although the name Amphictyones eventually prevailed over Amphictiones. In the narrator’s time they numbered thirty members representing several Greek peoples and cities.

l: Phocians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The Phocians seized the temple and were excluded from the Amphictyonic Council after the Sacred War ended. When Brennus led the Galati against Delphi, the Phocians fought more bravely than any other Greeks and were restored to the Council and to their former position in other respects.

l: Macedonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The Macedonians were admitted to the Amphictyonic Council after the Council was changed following the Sacred War. In the narrator’s time they supplied six of the Council’s members.
